figure.title: Figure: New lots per year
figure.takeaway: New lots in Campbelltown more than doubled while lower minimum lot sizes applied, from 351 in 2014 to a peak of 743 in 2017, then fell back to around the control-council average after the reform was reversed.
figure.caption: Campbelltown's new lots rose sharply while lower minimum lot sizes applied and fell back after the reversal. Control is the average of six inner and middle Adelaide councils. 2025 is probably a part-year.

workingPapers.abstract: What happens when part of a city cuts minimum lot sizes? We study a 2014 reform where a council in Adelaide cut them from 350 sqm to as low as 150 sqm, until the policy was partly reversed in 2019. The reform increased building approvals by 67 per cent, driven entirely by townhouses and rowhouses; the reversal returned the treatment effect to insignificant levels, providing dose-response evidence that lot-size regulation was a binding constraint. Established local firms already producing medium-density housing primarily built the new homes, with no evidence of capacity diversion. Movers into new housing were predominantly households in their prime family-formation years, upgrading out of cheaper rental housing. Using linked Census microdata, we trace the movement chains they set off: each mover typically vacates a cheaper dwelling, occupied by a household further down the income distribution. Chains also track the lifecycle: occupants further along the chain are younger and more often renting, with age composition explaining part of the income gradient. Concerns about amenity costs drove the reform’s reversal; across the outcomes we can measure we find little deterioration.

citedBy.title: Construction Productivity, The AI Plan, and Investment in Data Centres and Energy

seeAlso.title: What Can Australia Learn from New Zealand About Construction Productivity?
Can Zoning Reform Increase Construction Productivity? Suggestive Evidence from New Zealand

figure.title: Figure: Construction productivity, NZ vs Australia
figure.takeaway: On a 3-year rolling average rebased to 2010 = 100, residential construction productivity in New Zealand has pulled ahead of Australia's since the mid-2010s: 104 versus 87 in 2023.
figure.caption: Real output per hour worked in residential construction, indexed to 100 in 2010.

workingPapers.abstract: Construction sector productivity has stagnated or declined across much of the developed world in recent decades. This paper highlights a notable exception: New Zealand in the 2010s, where labour and multifactor productivity in construction each rose by over 15%. These gains were concentrated in building construction and closely aligned with the timing of widespread zoning reforms permitting medium- and high-density housing in three regions. A simple estimate suggests zoning reform increased Auckland's construction productivity by approximately 8%. I present evidence that upzoning drove productivity through four channels: (a) substantially increased dwellings completed per worker, which more than doubled in Auckland; (b) shifting construction towards higher-productivity regions; (c) increased competition by facilitating a more accessible medium-density construction market; and (d) raising average firm size in residential construction. While other partial explanations for New Zealand's construction productivity boom exist, these complement rather than contradict the role of zoning reform. Zoning reform offers a practical strategy for governments aiming to boost construction productivity.

publications.title: Dispelling Myths: Reviewing the Evidence on Zoning Reforms in Auckland

citedBy.title: Beyond Skepticism: Data Confirms Auckland's Zoning Reforms Delivered on Housing Promises

seeAlso.title: A Response to Murray and Helm on Auckland's Upzoning

publications.abstract: In 2016, the city of Auckland adopted zoning reforms that enabled more housing on approximately three-quarters of its urban land. Three subsequent studies have found that these reforms increased housing supply and reduced rents. Two economists have, however, criticised these studies on blogs and social media, describing their findings as a “myth”. Despite their informal nature, these critiques have been cited in formal planning and policy processes. Here, we review these critiques and find them to have little to no merit. Specifically, the critiques misunderstand the papers’ methods and rely on inappropriate analyses. In our view, there is remarkably robust evidence that zoning reforms increased housing supply and reduced rents in Auckland.

figure.title: Figure: Lower Hutt vs synthetic control
figure.takeaway: After Plan Change 43 in 2017, dwelling consents in Lower Hutt rose far above its synthetic control, reaching 12.2 per 1,000 residents in 2022 against 3.2 for synthetic Lower Hutt.
figure.caption: Dwelling consents per 1,000 residents. Synthetic Lower Hutt is a weighted mix of other councils that tracks Lower Hutt's consents before the 2017 upzoning.
figure.source: Maltman and Greenaway-McGrevy (2025); Stats NZ building consents.

publications.abstract: This paper studies a sequence of zoning reforms enacted in Lower Hutt, a constituent municipality of the wider Wellington metropolitan region of New Zealand. Beginning in the late 2010s, Lower Hutt independently implemented a sequence of widespread zoning changes to enable medium- and high-density housing in residential areas. Using a synthetic control to specify the policy counterfactual, we find that these zoning changes generated a three-fold increase in consents per capita and nearly tripled the number of housing starts over the six years subsequent to the onset of the reforms. Depending on how potential displacement effects are accounted for, the Lower Hutt reforms increased housing starts across the wider metropolitan region by approximately 10 to 18%. We also present evidence that the upzonings reduced rents by around 21% relative to the counterfactual.

publications.title: Perverse Policy Incentives and Inferior Economic Outcomes
publications.abstract: Between 1999 and 2012, Australia enacted a raft of policies that advantaged overseas students when applying for permanent residency, through the so-called 880 visa series. These policies greatly enhanced prospective students’ prospects to secure permanent residency when pursuing specific qualifications. Leveraging rich longitudinal administrative data linked to the universe of permanent visas issued in Australia, we analyse the economic implications of these historically skewed policy incentives. We document significant negative migrant selection. 880 migrants attracted lower incomes and exhibited lower probabilities of employment in high-skilled occupations, when compared to both migrants educated overseas as well as domestic students. 880 migrants achieved superior aggregate employment outcomes however, particularly in lower-skilled occupations unrelated to their fields of study. If visa streams are poorly designed therefore, any potential benefits of onshore education risk being crowded out by negative migrant selection.
